newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark backs down over Rushdie visit.
newsitem.headline: Denmark backs down over Rushdie visit.

text.p: Denmark bowed to international pressure on Friday and invited British writer Salman Rushdie to fly to Copenhagen to receive a European literary award.
The Danish authorities had originally cited security concerns for barring Rushdie, who faces a death threat from Iran over his novel "The Satanic Verses."
They were worried about advance publicity over a planned awards ceremony and said police were being too stretched by a Nordic biker gang war to offer sufficient protection.
Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and with permanent protection since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa against him.
Danish Culture Minister Jytte Hilten has invited Rushdie to come to Copenhagen to accept the award at some time before the New Year.
She wrote to him saying that the Danish government "regrets the award ceremony cannot take place as planned but must assure you that the decision was taken solely on security grounds.
"I would like to invite you and personally present you with your prize in Copenhagen," Hilden wrote.
Hilden's move came after the government came under a heavy barrage of criticism for barring Rushdie. Journalists and authors in Denmark, Sweden and Britain attacked the decision.
Rushdie, welcoming the news in London, told BBC Television: "Security objections seem to have fizzled out. I'm very pleased."

"I gather there's been a lot of fuss in Denmark today, and a lot of people (have been) very annoyed about the government's decision. I'm delighted that they have so swiftly reversed their decision," he said.
Presentation of awards to Rushdie, Austrian writer Christoph Ransmayer and Danish author and translator Thorkild Bjoernvig was originally to have made on November 14 in Copenhagen.
It is this year's European Cultural Capital, a title which rotates around the EU.
In the past two years Rushdie has travelled widely abroad and in Britain, giving lectures and attending literary events.
Iran says it is powerless to lift the fatwa, which can only be revoked by the man who issued it. But Khomeini died in 1989.
The European Union has made headway on blunting the fatwa since France launched a diplomatic initiative almost two years ago when it held the EU's rotating presidency.

Tehran says it would not send anyone to kill the author. But European officials say this would probably be insufficient to solve the long-running crisis without a further commitment to prevent others from doing so.
Rushdie says the dialogue has not gone far enough.

"The EU, although it has been very determined orally to get agreements, has put very few teeth into that process", he said on a visit this week to Vienna when he discussed with Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky how to step up pressure on Iran.
Rushdie, born to Moslem parents in Bombay, has always rejected Iran's charge of blasphemy against Islam.
